  • Older age (adult)
  • Male sex (not female)
  • Obesity
  • Edentulous
  • Facial hair (especially beard)
  • Mallampati class 3 or 4
  • Inability to protrude the mandible
  • Short thyromental distance
  • Snoring (indication of OSA)
  • Abnormal neck anatomy or mobility
  • -

Question: Which of the following is not a risk factor for difficult intubation?

options.name: Head and neck extension <30 degrees from neutral

description:
• Risk factors for difficult intubation include:
  • Prior difficult intubation
  • Interincisor gap <4 cm
  • Thyromental distance <6 cm
  • Sternomental distance <12 cm
  • Head and neck extension <30 degrees from neutral
  • Mallampati class III or IV
  • Inadequate mandibular protrusion or Upper Lip Bite Test Class III (not Class II)
  • Neck circumference >40 cm
  • Upper Lip Bite Test Class II is not a risk factor.
  • -

Question: Which of the following is risk factor for difficult LMA insertion?

options.name: Head and neck extension <30 degrees from neutral

description:
• Risk factors for difficult LMA insertion include:
  • Male gender (not female)
  • Obesity (BMI >30 kg/m²)
  • Poor dentition or large incisors
  • Neck radiation history
  • Reduced mouth opening
  • Reduced cervical spine motion
  • Tonsillar hypertrophy
  • Glottic, hypopharyngeal, and subglottic pathology
  • -

Question: Which of the following can make difficult videolaryngoscopy?
description:
• Risk factors for difficult videolaryngoscopy include:
  • Otolaryngologic and cardiac surgery
  • Sniffing head positioning
  • Abnormal neck anatomy (a neck scar, a neck mass, neck radiation changes)
  • Decreased cervical spine motion
  • Decreased oral entry (obesity, decreased mouth opening, decreased jaw mobility)
  • Restricted oropharyngeal space (edema, bleeding, retrognathia)
  • Neck circumference >40 cm is a risk factor.
  • -

Question: Which of the following is not component of obesity surgery mortality score?
description:
• Obesity surgery mortality risk score components (1 point each):
  • BMI >50 kg/m²
  • Male gender
  • Age >45 (not >65)
  • Hypertension
  • Risk factors for pulmonary thromboembolism (prior venous thromboembolism, vena cava filter, hypoventilation, pulmonary hypertension)
  • -

Question: The CDC and WHO classification of class 1 obesity falls between which body mass index (BMI)?
description:
• Underweight – BMI <18.5 kg/m²
  • Normal weight – BMI ≥18.5 to 24.9 kg/m²
  • Overweight – BMI ≥25 to 29.9 kg/m²
  • Obesity – Class 1 – BMI 30 to 34.9 kg/m²
  • Class 2 – BMI 35 to 39.9 kg/m²
  • Class 3 – BMI ≥40 kg/m²
  • -

Question: Which of the following BMI has risk of morbidity and mortality comparable to patients with normal body mass index (BMI)?
description:
• Otherwise healthy patients who are overweight and those with class 1 obesity (BMI 30 to 34.9 kg/m²) do not have an increased risk of most major adverse outcomes following noncardiac surgery compared with patients with normal body mass index (BMI), with the exception of venous thromboembolism.
  • This has been called the "obesity paradox."
  • -

Question: Which is false statement when assessing a patient with COPD for any elective surgery during preanesthetic evaluation?

options.name: Patient with stable COPD does not require any further evaluation for his lung condition
Patient with COPD with active symptoms needs CXR to evaluate
Patient with COPD not at their pulmonary baseline Requires PFT

Question: In a cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET), which of the following best describes the physiological event known as the Anaerobic Threshold?

options.name: The exercise intensity where lactic acid production exceeds clearance rates.
The point at which heart rate reaches 85% of predicted maximum.
The onset of total muscle anoxia (0% oxygen).

description:
• Anaerobic threshold (AT) , also known as the lactate threshold or the ventilatory threshold, represents the point at which lactate accumulation exceeds lactate clearance during exercise.
  • The AT is thought to represent the shift to anaerobic metabolism during exercise.
  • AT normally occurs at more than 40 percent of maximal predicted V̇O₂.
  • -

Question: The Modified Borg Scale is most commonly used for:

options.name: Evaluating acute dyspnea intensity during exertion or in the ED.
Measuring the emotional impact of dyspnea over the last week.
Determining the prognosis of interstitial lung disease.

description:
• The Modified Borg Scale is most commonly used for evaluating acute dyspnea intensity during exertion or in the emergency department.
  • -

Question: All of the following can cause chronic dyspnea except
description:
• The five most common causes of chronic dyspnea are:
  • Asthma
  • Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
  • Interstitial lung disease
  • Myocardial dysfunction
  • Obesity/deconditioning
  • Therefore, none of the options are exceptions (all can cause chronic dyspnea).
  • -

Question: In a patient with iron-deficiency anemia scheduled for surgery in less than 2 weeks, which treatment is most appropriate?
description:
• For patients scheduled for surgery in less than 2 weeks, intravenous (IV) iron is the most appropriate treatment for iron-deficiency anemia as it works faster than oral iron.
  • Oral ferrous sulfate takes too long to be effective within 2 weeks.
  • -

Question: Which of the following patients is not considered to have suppression of their HPA axis and therefore does not require routine perioperative glucocorticoid coverage?

options.name: Patient on inhaled fluticasone 1000 microgm/day for 6 months

description:
• The following groups of patients do not need additional perioperative glucocorticoid coverage:
  • Any patient who has been taking any dose of glucocorticoid for less than three weeks
  • Patients who have received morning doses of less than 5 mg/day of prednisone or its equivalent for any length of time
  • Patients being treated with less than 10 mg of prednisone or its equivalent every other day
  • Inhaled corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone) are considered to have minimal systemic absorption and do not cause HPA axis suppression at standard doses.
  • -

Question: Which of the following patient scenarios is considered at HIGH risk for HPA axis suppression, requiring stress-dose steroids?
description:
• Suppressed HPA axis patients include:
  • Any patient who is currently taking more than 20 mg/day of prednisone or its equivalent for more than three weeks
  • Any patient on glucocorticoids who has clinical Cushing syndrome
  • Prednisone 30 mg daily for 1 month meets both criteria (>20 mg/day and >3 weeks).
  • -

Question: What is the recommended stress-dose steroid coverage for a patient undergoing major surgery (e.g., cardiac bypass)?

options.name: Hydrocortisone 50-100 mg IV immediately, then 50 mg every 8 hours.

description:
• For major surgical stress (e.g., esophagogastrectomy, total proctocolectomy, open heart surgery):
  • Take usual morning steroid dose.
  • Give 100 mg of intravenous hydrocortisone before induction of anesthesia and 50 mg every eight hours for 24 hours.
  • Taper dose by half per day to maintenance level.
  • -

Question: Which medication is preferred for IV stress-dose steroid coverage?
description:
• Hydrocortisone is preferred due to its rapid onset and both mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid effects.
  • -

Question: How long should "stress-dose" steroids typically be continued after surgery?

options.name: 24–48 hours, followed by a rapid taper.

description:
• Steroids are typically continued for 24–48 hours after surgery, followed by a rapid taper back to the maintenance dose to minimize side effects.
  • -

Question: A patient has been on chronic steroids for 1 year, but a morning cortisol test a week before surgery was (>15 mcg/dl). Do they need stress-dose steroids?

options.name: No, they have an intact HPA axis.
Only if they are having major surgery.

description:
• Patients with an early morning cortisol level >10 mcg/dL (275 nmol/L) likely do not have a significant impairment of the HPA axis and may be continued on their current glucocorticoid replacement dose on the day of surgery. Such patients do not need additional perioperative glucocorticoid therapy.
  • -

Question: A 55-year-old patient on prednisone (5 mg) daily for chronic joint pain is scheduled for a total knee arthroplasty (moderate stress). What is the most appropriate perioperative steroid management?

options.name: No extra steroids needed; continue usual daily dose.
Give IV hydrocortisone at induction, then a maintained schedule for 48 hours.
Give IV hydrocortisone at induction, then resume home dose.
High-dose supplementation is required to prevent immediate adrenal crisis.

description:
• Patients currently taking doses of 5 to 20 mg of prednisone (or its equivalent) for more than three weeks have considerable variability in HPA axis suppression.
  • For moderate surgical stress (e.g., total joint replacement):
  • Take usual morning steroid dose.
  • Give 50 mg hydrocortisone intravenously just before the procedure and 25 mg of hydrocortisone every eight hours for 24 hours.
  • Resume usual dose thereafter.
  • -

Question: According to current evidence, which of the following is considered the best strategy for managing a patient with "indeterminate risk" who is undergoing minor surgery (e.g., hernia repair)?

options.name: Start high-dose intravenous hydrocortisone immediately and taper over 5 days.
Double the dose of steroids on the morning of surgery only.

description:
• For minor procedures or surgery under local anesthesia (e.g., inguinal hernia repair):
  • Take usual morning steroid dose.
  • No extra supplementation is necessary.
  • -

Question: A patient undergoing emergency hip surgery under spinal anesthesia suddenly develops hypotension, tachycardia, and a reduced level of consciousness. The patient has a history of long-term steroid use. After ensuring adequate fluid resuscitation, what is the best next step?

options.name: Proceed with surgery as fast as possible.

description:
• Patients who require urgent or emergency surgery who have taken glucocorticoids but the degree of HPA axis suppression is unknown should receive empiric perioperative glucocorticoid coverage.
  • The recommended regimen for major surgical stress is 100 mg of intravenous hydrocortisone before induction.
  • Delaying surgery to perform evaluation of the HPA axis would be inappropriate in this setting.
